content: 1. National Coverage and Quality of Vital Registration Systems: To meet the required standard, two benchmarks must be satisfied: The cause of death must be documented in at least 90% of all recorded deaths, either through a national vital registration system or a sample-based system. Less than 10% of deaths should be assigned ill-defined causes, as per ICD-9 codes 780-799 or ICD-10 codes R00-R99. 2. Assessment of Surveillance Systems: Surveillance systems must be evaluated against specific benchmarks to determine whether they meet, partially meet, or fail to meet the standards. This includes documenting key results, recommending actions to improve system quality, and estimating budgets for necessary improvements. 3. Drug-Resistant TB Surveillance: This can be achieved by documenting rifampicin susceptibility status (positive/negative) for at least 75% of new pulmonary TB cases or through a nationally representative drug resistance survey. 4. HIV Prevalence in TB Cases: This requires documenting HIV status (positive/negative) for at least 80% of all notified TB cases or obtaining representative data from settings with low-level HIV epidemics. 5. Consistency with WHO Guidelines: TB case definitions must align with WHO guidelines. This includes distinguishing laboratory-confirmed cases from clinically diagnosed cases, differentiating new cases from previously treated cases, and separating pulmonary from extrapulmonary cases. 6. Minimum Data Variables for TB Cases: Surveillance systems must routinely collect data on the following variables for all TB cases: Age or age group Sex Year of registration Bacteriological results History of previous treatment Anatomical site of disease Patient identifier (for case-based systems) 7. Internal Consistency of Surveillance Data: Data should be internally consistent over time. This includes maintaining consistent ratios of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases, male-to-female TB cases, and childhood TB cases. Year-to-year changes in case notification rates should also be monitored. 8. Vital Registration Data for TB Mortality: If available, vital registration data should provide national-level TB mortality rates (HIV-negative TB). If not, national TB case data disaggregated by age, sex, and disease type should be used to monitor trends over the past five years. 9. Data Completeness and Reporting: For paper-based systems, quarterly reports from basic management units (BMUs) should be aggregated and submitted. For electronic systems, data files from sub-national databases must be imported into the national database. 10. Accuracy and Completeness of Quarterly Reports: For paper-based systems, quarterly reports must be accurate, complete, and internally consistent. Sub-totals of TB cases by age, sex, and case type should match the total number of reported cases in at least 95% of reports. 11. Recommended Actions for Improvement: Budgets should be allocated to address gaps and implement necessary changes. 12. Examples of Implementation: In Kenya, TB case definitions are consistent with WHO guidelines, and surveillance systems meet the required standards. In the USA, the electronic case-based TB surveillance system spans all states and territories, meeting all benchmarks. The system distinguishes pulmonary from extrapulmonary cases and uses hierarchical case classification criteria. 13. Challenges and Limitations: Common challenges include underreporting, delays in data aggregation, and incomplete data from non-reporting units. Paper-based systems may fail to capture all required variables, particularly for smear-positive cases. 14. Future Recommendations: Countries should consider transitioning to electronic case-based systems to improve data accuracy and completeness. Routine cross-checking of TB registers and enforcing zero-case reporting are essential to minimize data gaps.
